evaluation.positioning_hook: A British fixer is pulled back by an old friend into a globe-spanning heist that turns out to be cover for exposing a corruption network and returning stolen wealth to its victims.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is easy to sell: an elite heist, international locations, and a moral reveal that re-frames the job as justice. It has clear mainstream appeal for adult thriller audiences, though the dense procedural detail and long runway to the true mission keep it from feeling four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands quickly in the New York bar scene, then sharpens into the Monaco/Ferrari/vault job and finally reveals the documentary takedown. The script is very explainable in two sentences, with a clean engine and a strong late-game turn.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Liam, Damian, Eleanor, Rico, Felix, and Milo each have a distinct function and voice, and the team chemistry is a real asset. The lead is solid rather than iconic, and the supporting players are vivid but still mostly orbit Damian's plan.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script's boldest move is making the heist a delivery system for whistleblower justice rather than pure theft. The execution is familiar in its caper grammar, but the moral architecture and the team banter give it a cleaner identity than a standard crime job movie.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps resetting with new locations, new targets, and escalating complications, from the wrong vault in Sardinia to the Swiss bathroom fight to the Hollywood Hills finale. The momentum is strong because each set piece changes the stakes rather than just repeating the same beat.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The central idea — a heist that is secretly a truth operation — feels fresh and commercially legible. It is not radically unprecedented, but the combination of caper mechanics, institutional corruption, and public-release payoff gives it a memorable moral spine.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The script builds a specific underworld of precision operators, private banking, Monaco logistics, and elite fixers with real texture. Andrea's island, the Grand Prix cover, the Swiss vault, and the Meridian backstory all make the world feel story-generating rather than decorative.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually confident: dry, polished, lightly comic, and operationally cool even when the plot is moving fast. The banter between the crew and the procedural confidence of the jobs give it a distinct upscale-caper register.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Damian's father, the Meridian fraud, and Liam's hidden skill set suggest a deeper history beneath the surface caper. The script does not over-explain the emotional engine, which helps, though the depth is still mostly concentrated in Damian rather than distributed across the ensemble.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: This is one of the script's strongest assets: Damian/Liam, Damian/Eleanor, Rico/Felix, and the whole-team friction all generate playable scenes. The group has enough internal chemistry that almost any pairing can carry a sequence.

lead_characters.name: Damian Cross
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 30s, British, elite criminal strategist with a personal stake in institutional fraud.
lead_characters.hook: Damian is the architect of the entire operation: controlled, obsessive, and emotionally sealed until the pressure leaks through. He is not chasing money so much as building a machine to expose the people who destroyed his father, and the script gives him the rare combination of competence, moral conviction, and dangerous secrecy that can anchor a star turn.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Fassbender in Steve Jobs or Tom Hardy in Locke — a hyper-competent man whose stillness, precision, and buried grief do the heavy lifting. The role gives an actor command, intelligence, and a late-film moral reveal that recontextualizes everything.

lead_characters.name: Liam Carter
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 30s, British, outsider with covert tactical skill and a guarded emotional life.
lead_characters.hook: Liam is the audience surrogate who gets pulled back into Damian's orbit and slowly reveals he is far more dangerous than he first appears. He reads as dry, observant, and self-protective, with the kind of understated competence that makes him feel like a man with a past the script is only partially unpacking.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Richard Madden in Bodyguard or Jon Hamm in Baby Driver a chance to play cool restraint with sudden physical authority. It offers a performer the pleasure of being the calm center in chaos, then revealing the hidden edge.

lead_characters.name: Eleanor Cross
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early 30s, British, forensic accountant, Damian's fiancée and operational equal.
lead_characters.hook: Eleanor is the smartest person in the room more often than not, and the script lets her be both romantic partner and strategic operator without flattening either side. She is precise, skeptical, emotionally direct, and one of the few people who can puncture Damian's self-mythology without losing his trust.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Emily Blunt in Sicario or Rebecca Ferguson in Mission: Impossible a chance to be the smartest, coolest person in the frame. It gives an actor authority, wit, and a relationship dynamic that is intimate without being ornamental.

lead_characters.name: Rico Santoro
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 30s, Latino, explosives specialist with a gruff, paternal edge.
lead_characters.hook: Rico is the blunt-force personality in the crew, but the script keeps giving him intelligence, warmth, and a surprisingly philosophical streak. He is funny, physically imposing, and deeply practical, which makes him feel like the kind of character who can steal scenes without ever trying to.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Benicio del Toro in Sicario or Michael Peña in End of Watch — a character actor role with swagger, humor, and real authority. It gives an actor the chance to be both the comic pressure valve and the guy you absolutely want on your side.

lead_characters.name: Felix Novak
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s, tech specialist, likely white or ethnically ambiguous, socially anxious and hyper-competent.
lead_characters.hook: Felix is the nervous system of the operation: fast, brilliant, slightly chaotic, and always one coffee away from a breakdown. The script makes his anxiety part of his charm, and his technical precision gives him a distinct rhythm in the ensemble.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network or Rami Malek in Mr. Robot a chance to turn speed, anxiety, and intelligence into a signature. It offers a performer a highly specific verbal cadence and a lot of scene-stealing utility.

lead_characters.name: Milo Reyes
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid 30s, Latino, driver/mechanic with a calm, grounded presence.
lead_characters.hook: Milo is the quiet professional: less flashy than Rico or Felix, but often the one who sounds most sane when the room gets noisy. He has a dry humor and a practical intelligence that makes him feel like the crew member everyone trusts when things go sideways.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded, cool supporting role that gave Oscar Isaac in Drive or Pedro Pascal in Triple Frontier a chance to play competence with warmth. It gives an actor understated charisma and a strong ensemble foothold.

lead_characters.name: Andrea Calcale
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s, Italian, wealthy fixer with criminal-adjacent influence and social ease.
lead_characters.hook: Andrea is the elegant wildcard: charming, dangerous, and always slightly amused by everyone else’s seriousness. He adds class, access, and a sense that the crew is moving through a world of people who can make problems disappear if they like you enough.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Stanley Tucci in The Devil Wears Prada or Javier Bardem in Skyfall a chance to dominate scenes with wit and menace. It offers a performer a deliciously controlled, high-status presence.

lead_characters.name: Agent Theadore Collins
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, federal agent, composed and methodical.
lead_characters.hook: Collins is the patient institutional counterweight: calm, strategic, and willing to wait three years for a payoff. He is not written as a cartoon antagonist, which gives him more weight in the final moral collision.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Shea Whigham or Michael Shannon a chance to play authority with pressure underneath it. It offers a performer quiet menace and procedural intelligence.

lead_characters.name: Agent Gabriel Morales
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid 30s, federal agent, observant and more emotionally open than his partner.
lead_characters.hook: Morales is the more human face of the FBI pressure, the one who can still register doubt and moral complexity. He functions as the audience's institutional conscience, which makes his scenes with Liam and Damian especially useful.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Diego Luna in Narcos: Mexico or Mahershala Ali in True Detective a chance to bring intelligence and empathy into a law-enforcement frame. It gives an actor restraint, nuance, and a strong final-act dialogue scene.

physical confidence required for Liam and Rico

notable_requirements: Los Angeles docks, tech center, parking garage, diner, safe house, Hollywood Hills mansion
Monaco estate, streets, and Grand Prix-adjacent exteriors
Swiss bank facility and safe house

technical.vfx_details: Mostly practical geography and crowd control; limited enhancement for Monaco race atmosphere, helicopter presence, and city-scale coverage.
technical.sfx_needs: Vault-door practical effects, controlled explosions, fight choreography in the bar and Swiss bathroom, vehicle loading and boat transfer mechanics.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: wide-to-platform thriller with strong streamer and specialty theatrical upside.

budget.note: Contemporary but geographically expansive: New York, Los Angeles, Rome, Sardinia, Monaco, Switzerland, plus race-day crowd work and multiple set-piece interiors. The car, boat, bank, and helicopter material are all scope-able, but the travel footprint and specialty locations keep this above a contained indie.

casting.note: The script lives or dies on the chemistry between Damian, Liam, Eleanor, Rico, Felix, and Milo, with each role needing a distinct comic-musical rhythm. Liam and Damian in particular need actors who can play cool competence, buried history, and moral tension without over-explaining it.

development.note: The late reveal that the heist is cover for a Meridian exposure operation is strong, but the script asks the audience to track a lot of moving parts before the true mission lands. The buyer conversation will center on whether the caper mechanics and the whistleblower payoff feel equally legible.

comp_set.title: Ocean's Eleven
comp_set.why_it_comps: The ensemble caper energy, polished banter, and pleasure of watching specialists execute a high-stakes plan are directly in that lane.

comp_set.title: The Italian Job
comp_set.why_it_comps: The vehicle-forward heist mechanics, international flavor, and cleanly staged team logistics echo this kind of crowd-pleasing crime movie.

comp_set.title: Triple Frontier
comp_set.why_it_comps: The crew dynamics, moral ambiguity, and sense that the job is bigger than the money place it close to this modern adult-action crime lane.

comp_set.title: Inside Man
comp_set.why_it_comps: The procedural intelligence, institutional target, and reveal-driven structure resemble the smart-heist architecture of this title.

comp_set.title: The Accountant
comp_set.why_it_comps: The cool, competence-first protagonist and the blend of precision, violence, and hidden agenda fit the same audience expectation.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like smart, stylish crime movies with ensemble banter and a moral payoff.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly male-skewing but accessible to women through the Damian/Eleanor relationship and the team chemistry, college-educated streamer/theatrical thriller audience.

budget_tier.note: Multiple international locations, race-day crowd scenes, practical vault work, vehicle logistics, and a moderate stunt/fight load push this into a mid-budget feature profile.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally with buyers who want a polished, adult crime movie that can travel internationally and sell on cast, concept, and execution. The ensemble, globe-trotting structure, and clean moral turn make it attractive to platforms and distributors looking for a smart crowd-pleaser with some prestige sheen.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the story resolves the Meridian operation and Damian's arc cleanly, and the supporting crew are vivid but not built as separate franchise anchors.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The heist is secretly a whistleblower operation.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the movie a built-in moral engine, which is a stronger commercial promise than a standard money-grab caper. It will attract buyers who want genre pleasure with a conscience and audiences who like their crime movies to end in public consequence, not just escape.
strengths.evidence: The Monaco vault and Ferrari job are later revealed as cover for exposing Meridian and returning stolen wealth to victims.

strengths.what_it_means: The script can sell on team dynamics, which broadens the appeal beyond the lead and gives the movie repeatable scene energy. That is exactly what producers want when they are packaging a mid-budget crime film around character rather than spectacle.
strengths.evidence: Rico, Felix, Milo, Eleanor, Damian, and Liam all have distinct rhythms in the bar, diner, flight, and planning scenes.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tone is polished and playable.
strengths.what_it_means: The dry banter and operational confidence make the script feel expensive and watchable even when the plot is doing complex work. That helps it sit in a premium-streamer lane where buyers want sophistication without heaviness.
strengths.evidence: The bar banter, the repeated jokes about left/right, and the crew's casual competence during high-pressure jobs.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world feels specific and saleable.
strengths.what_it_means: Monaco, Sardinia, Zurich, Hollywood Hills, and the Grand Prix give the movie a global sheen that reads as premium without requiring tentpole scale. That is useful for international buyers and for marketing a crime movie that needs visual distinction.
strengths.evidence: The Monaco qualifying-day heist, Andrea's island base, and the Swiss bank sequence all add texture and geography.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Damian is a strong anchor role.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead has intelligence, control, and a late-film moral reveal, which is the kind of part that can attract a serious actor and elevate the package. That matters because a mid-budget crime film often gets greenlit on the strength of one magnetic central performance.
strengths.evidence: Damian's quiet planning, his history with his father, and the jail-cell monologue that reframes the entire operation.

whats_special.headline: This is a polished, adult crime caper with a real commercial twist: the heist is cover for a public takedown, which gives the movie a cleaner moral hook than the usual genre package. Add a strong ensemble, international locations, and a lead role built for a serious actor, and you have a mid-budget thriller that can sell to streamers and theatrical buyers alike.

items.detail: For a long stretch, the script plays as a globe-trotting heist before the Meridian exposure plan becomes fully clear. That delay is workable, but it means the buyer conversation will focus on whether the audience stays locked in before the moral engine is fully visible.

items.area: The geography asks for a lot.
items.detail: New York, Los Angeles, Rome, Sardinia, Monaco, Switzerland, and Hollywood Hills all appear on the page, with race-day coverage and multiple specialty interiors. That is still producible, but it pushes the movie away from a clean contained-thriller buy and into a more managed mid-budget conversation.

Rico, Felix, Milo, Eleanor, Damian, and Liam all need to feel distinct and musically timed, because the script leans hard on banter and group dynamics. If the cast is merely competent instead of electric, a lot of the movie's lift disappears.

items.area: The FBI thread is a little underpowered.
items.detail: Collins and Morales function well as pressure, but their investigation is mostly a framing device until the final reveal. That keeps the story moving, though it also means the institutional side of the conflict is less textured than the crew side.

issues.headline: The main friction is structural, not tonal: the movie spends a long time as a stylish heist before the deeper Meridian payoff fully clicks into place. On top of that, the international footprint and chemistry-dependent ensemble mean this is a package that needs the right cast and a disciplined production plan to land at its best.
